findings.statement: Membership fee revenue increased 11% in 2026, and renewal rates at year end were 92.3% in the U.S. and Canada and 89.8% worldwide.
findings.rationale: Both parts of the claim are covered: fee income rose and renewal rates are high.

quotes.text: Membership fee revenue increased 11% in 2026, driven by new member sign-ups, membership fee increases, and upgrades to Executive memberships. At the end of 2026, member renewal rates were 92.3% in the U.S. and Canada and 89.8% worldwide.

findings.statement: Part of the fee income growth came from the fee increase rather than from renewals alone: the increase accounted for approximately 30% and 40% of membership income growth during 2026 and 2025.
findings.rationale: The growth is not purely from members renewing, which tempers how much it shows about loyalty.

quotes.text: The fee income increase accounted for approximately 30% and 40% of membership income growth during 2026 and 2025.

findings.statement: The worldwide renewal rate is adversely impacted by international membership growth and by online-sold memberships, which renew at a slightly lower rate on average.
findings.rationale: This names a mix effect that could pull renewal rates down, a caveat to 'keep paying to re-up'.

quotes.text: Our worldwide renewal rate is adversely impacted by membership growth in certain international markets and a higher penetration of memberships sold online, including through digital membership promotions, which renew at a slightly lower rate on average.

response.rationale: The filing reports 11% growth in membership fee revenue and high renewal rates, which supports the claim. Some of the growth is attributed to a fee increase and the worldwide renewal rate faces mix headwinds, but nothing in the passages says fee income is no longer climbing.
unknowns: The prior-year renewal rates, so the direction of the renewal trend cannot be read.
